The past decade has witnessed the rapid growth of pilot studies and the adoption of drone-assisted delivery by
many e-commerce companies. In practice, delivery companies usually assemble fleets of drones consisting of
heterogeneous configurations to satisfy various customer package demands, and this calls for in-depth research
on how to deliver packages via drones efficiently. In this study, we extend the classic vehicle routing problem
(VRP) by optimally scheduling the operations in a package depot center with a fleet of drones with different
capacities, speeds, and maximum flight ranges. The drones travel multiple sorties to serve customers nearby.
We formulate this problem as a mixed integer programming (MIP) model that minimizes the total delivery
time for a set of packages. Due to the NP-hardness of the problem, we first develop a FIFO-based genetic
algorithm (FBGA) to solve the problem. In anticipation of multiple trips, we further propose a modified,
rescheduling-based genetic algorithm (RBGA) that incorporates a small-scale routing-planning optimization
model that ‘‘reschedules’’ drone operations at the end of drone sorties, with the objective of minimizing the
completion time. The RBGA features the combination of the knapsack problem, the shortest path problem, and
a scheduling problem, from which near-optimal delivery plans are obtained for the fleet of drones. We conduct
extensive numerical experiments with different numbers of customers and drones to evaluate the performance
of the algorithms. The results suggest that compared with MIP, the proposed algorithms solve the problem
efficiently for the testing instances, particularly for large instances that MIP fails to solve in time, indicating
the practicality of the proposed methods for real-world implementations.

In fact, many studies have been focusing on improving the vehicle

especially on their flight range. For example, Dorling et al. (2017)
consider the drone routing problem with multiple trips under a linear
relationship between energy consumption and drone capacity. Song,
Park, and Kim (2018) optimize the delivery with capacity limita-

to its shortened flight range, which suggests modeling drone energy

instead. Considering the limited life of the drones’ batteries, in many

affect the battery consumption rate (BCR). Neglecting the impact of
these factors to BCR could potentially cause the drone to run out of
power halfway (Torabbeigi, Lim, & Kim, 2020), resulting in package
damage or loss. Besides, energy consumption will also affect the drone’s
speed (Raj & Murray, 2020), which will affect the actual delivery time.

widely researched solution is the coordinated use of both trucks and
drones. Bouman, Agatz, and Schmidt (2018), de Freitas and Penna
(2020), Murray and Chu (2015) and Murray and Raj (2020). In such
cases, drones are carried by trucks, the delivery range is hence ex-
panded, and the impact of changeable capacity and speed become less
significant. The type of coordinated delivery approach also benefits
from the drones’ capability to fly over obstacles like rivers and low-
rise buildings, saving the total delivery time compared with truck-only
deliveries. However, similar to traditional delivery approaches, the
truck-drone coordinated delivery still heavily relies on the local road
network, where traffic congestion could delay the delivery by hours.

Furthermore, recent progress in technology has enabled the recharg-
ing of drone batteries, allowing for extended delivery capabilities by
permitting drones to return to the depot for recharging and execut-
ing additional delivery tasks (Hassanalian & Abdelkefi, 2017). The
literature has seen a wealth of studies on the scheduling of drone
deliveries, including the use of battery charging or replacement, in
order to mitigate the limitations of their limited payload capacity and
flight range. For example, Sundar and Rathinam (2013) explored the
shortest path for a drone to visit all targets by allowing for refueling to
extend the flight distance, considering one drone and multiple depots
in a VRP. Gonzalez, Canca, Andrade-Pineda, Calle, and Leon-Blanco
(2020) proposed the use of a truck as a ‘‘recharging station’’, where
drones could return to for another trip. Despite the limited capacity and
flight range of each drone, efficient delivery can be achieved through
multiple short-distance deliveries. Liu, Chen, Li, and Liu (2021) studied
the scheduling of multiple homogeneous drones in one depot, where
drones can change batteries at the depot after completing a delivery
to avoid the problems caused by carrying only a few packages for
short-distance delivery each time.
However, to the best of our knowledge, few have studied the
scheduling problem of heterogeneous drones with multiple trips. In
this study, we consider the drone delivery problem where a fleet
of heterogeneous, rechargeable drones deliver packages to customers
through multiple trips. We model this problem using mixed integer
programming (MIP), which has been widely used in many other similar
studies (Murray & Chu, 2015; Murray & Raj, 2020).
Due to the NP-hardness of the classic grounded VRP, drone-based
VRP with additional constraints like capacity and flight range is also
NP-hard (Wang, Poikonen, & Golden, 2017). As a result, MIP models
usually scale poorly when the size of the problem increases and often
become intractable for large-scale implementations. As such, many
studies in the literature have contributed to various algorithms aiming
to obtain faster solutions, such as branch-and-cut (Tamke & Buscher,
2021), neighborhood search (Ropke & Pisinger, 2006), simulated an-
nealing (Dorling et al., 2017) and others heuristics (Kim, Lim, Cho, &
Côté, 2017; Kitjacharoenchai et al., 2019; Toth & Vigo, 2002). How-
ever, the research on combining heterogeneous drones with multiple
trips has not been fully explored. Thus, in this study, we develop
a Genetic Algorithm (GA) by incorporating a small-scale IP model
with only binary variables that expertly ‘‘reschedules’’ drone operations
when drones have completed their sorties. The rescheduling-based
GA features the combination of a knapsack problem, a shortest-path
problem, and a scheduling problem, from which near-optimal delivery
plans are obtained for the fleet of drones.
The main contributions of this study are as follows. First, we ex-
tend the traditional drone delivery problem by allowing heterogeneous
drones with different flight ranges, capacities, and speeds, which per-
form multiple trips after changing batteries at the depot. Second,
we formulate the problem as an MIP model to optimize the shortest
delivery time. Third, we develop a rescheduling-based GA that solves
the problem effectively. Last but not least, we conduct extensive nu-
merical experiments to show the advantages of the proposed algorithms
compared with the benchmark solution obtained by Gurobi. Sensitive
analysis is conducted to compare how different types of drones’ flight
ranges, capacities, and speeds affect the delivery tasks.
This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formally de-
fine the problem along with pertinent assumptions. We then develop
the MIP formulation of the problem. In Section 3, we first present
a traditional GA and then improve it through a rescheduling-based
process. In Section 4, we conduct different experiments to evaluate
the performance of the proposed methods. In Section 5, we draw
conclusions and discuss further research directions.

5. Conclusion
This study extends the classical VRP by considering drone-assisted
eliveries. Based on drones’ capacity and speed, we consider a single
hub that contains multiple types of drones, and each drone can deliver
goods for many sorties by changing batteries in the hub. An MIP
model is formulated, and we first propose a FIFO-based GA to solve
the model due to its NP-hardness. When multiple flights are allowed,
an IP model is developed to determine which drones need to deliver
packages again after it returns to the hub. The underlying problem
becomes a combination of the knapsack problem, the shortest path
problem, and the scheduling problem. We then develop a rescheduling-
based GA to help it adapt to large-scale instances with multiple trips.
Numerical experiments show that these two heuristic algorithms can
find sub-optimal solutions for small instances when compared with
commercial solvers. For large-scale instances, the proposed algorithms
are able to solve problems with up to 100 customers within a reason-
able computational time for potential practical applications. With the
scale increasing, the FBGA is robust with a very minor increase in the
solution time, while the RBGA yields better solutions than the FIFO-
based GA, at the cost of a longer solution time as it has to solve the
embedded IP problem.

Future directions for this research include incorporating more re-
alistic considerations into the drone vehicle routing problem, such as
the cost of battery replacements, the rate of energy consumption, and
battery replacement strategies. Additionally, the current study focuses
on a fixed set of packages that do not change during delivery, but
in reality, new packages may arrive after the delivery plan has been
established. It is therefore of interest to explore how to dynamically
update the delivery plan in such scenarios. Finally, incorporating pack-
age priorities and due dates into the model could provide even greater
insight into real-world drone delivery operations.
